prompts.q: Name an outcome of effective HRM
prompts.hint: Think of what goes UP (skills, motivation) and what goes DOWN (the CLAW ABC problems).
prompts.learn: The strategic role of HR is managing the total employer-employee relationship so the workforce adds value and the business reaches its goals. Effective HRM shows up as a skilled, motivated workforce with low disputes, absenteeism and turnover.

answers.why: Effective HRM motivates staff, and motivated staff are more productive.
Ineffective HRM causes dissatisfaction and low morale; effective HRM reverses it.
Good acquisition and training build skills, so work gets done more efficiently.
Staff stay longer, avoiding the cost of constantly replacing leavers.
Engaged, satisfied staff take fewer unplanned days off.
Good HR practices mean fewer grievances, less industrial action and lower dispute costs.
Good WHS management cuts accidents, sick leave and insurance premiums.
Keeping good staff means spending less on recruiting, inducting and paying out leavers.

prompts.q: Give a way HR and Marketing depend on each other
prompts.hint: Customer service, sales training, and who makes the job ads look good.
prompts.learn: Interdependence means each key business function relies on the others. Marketing needs HR to hire, train and motivate customer-facing staff, and HR needs Marketing's branding and input to recruit.

answers.a: Motivated staff give better customer service
answers.why: HR motivates staff, and motivated staff serve customers better.

answers.a: HR recruits and retains marketing staff
answers.why: Marketing depends on HR to attract, retain and train its marketing workers.

answers.a: Training sales staff in customer service
answers.why: Personal selling and relationship marketing rely on staff HR has trained in customer service.
Satisfied employees interact better with customers, improving satisfaction and loyalty.
HR consults Marketing to write accurate role and job descriptions when hiring marketing staff.

answers.a: Marketing brands recruitment ads and website
answers.why: HR depends on Marketing for branding on recruitment ads and the careers website.

near.msg: Funding for HR comes from Finance, not Marketing.

prompts.q: Give a way HR and Finance depend on each other
prompts.hint: Follow the money: what does HR need funds for? And who hires the accountants?
prompts.learn: Finance provides the budgets HR needs to recruit, train, reward and separate staff, while Finance relies on HR to attract, retain and train its own workers.

answers.why: HR can only act within the budget and funds Finance allocates to it.
Advertising, agency fees and selection all need money from Finance.
Training programs are paid for out of the budget Finance provides.
Finance funds wages plus monetary and non-monetary benefits.

answers.a: HR recruits and trains finance staff
answers.why: Finance depends on HR to attract, retain and train its finance workers.
Separation costs such as redundancy payouts must be budgeted by Finance.
HR consults Finance to formulate accurate role descriptions when sourcing finance staff.

near.msg: Branding for recruitment ads comes from Marketing, not Finance.

prompts.q: Give a way HR and Operations depend on each other
prompts.hint: New technology, productivity, safety and the right skills.
prompts.learn: Operations relies on HR for skilled, trained and motivated production staff, and HR must manage the people side of operational change such as new technology and WHS.

answers.why: HR's training, development and motivation strategies drive operations productivity.
HR must recruit staff with the skills and experience needed to produce the product.
HR and Operations work together to implement and comply with WHS legislation.
New operations technology may force HR to restructure jobs and manage the change process.
When technology replaces workers, HR runs the redundancy and separation processes.
HR monitors the performance of production employees and runs training to close gaps.

near.msg: Budgets come from Finance; Operations depends on HR for people, skills and safety.

prompts.q: Name an HR function a business could outsource
prompts.hint: Payroll is the classic one. Think of every job an HR department does.
prompts.learn: Outsourcing HR means using external providers (contractors, domestic or global) for some or all HR activities, to access specialist skills, lower costs and focus on core business.

answers.why: Payroll is a support and compliance task commonly handed to specialist providers.
Recruitment agencies and headhunters can source and screen applicants.
External trainers deliver off-the-job courses and specialist skills training.
Contractors can run leadership training for current and future managers.
Specialists can design and run appraisal and performance management systems.
An outside mediator can help resolve workplace disputes neutrally.
HRIS software and support can be provided by external technology firms.
Consultants can guide staff through restructures and other major change.
Contractors can write and update HR policies to keep them legally compliant.

near.msg: Businesses keep core functions in-house; outsourcing is for support activities so they can focus on the core.

prompts.q: Give an advantage of outsourcing HR functions
prompts.hint: Core, costs, expertise... and domestic vs global contractors each have their own pluses.
prompts.learn: Outsourcing uses external contractors to perform HR activities, letting the business focus on core functions and access specialist expertise at lower cost. Domestic contractors know local law; global contractors can offer cheaper labour and advanced technology.

answers.why: Handing off support work like payroll frees management to focus on the core business.
Providers bring expert skills in support and compliance work such as payroll.
Outsourcing is often cheaper than running the function in-house.
Domestic contractors are used to avoid employing extra in-house staff and their overheads.
A domestic contractor already knows Australian employment law.
Domestic contractors avoid the language and cultural misunderstandings of global ones.
Global contractors work under different employment standards, which can cut labour costs.
Global providers may offer more advanced HR technology and faster service.
You can visit and inspect a domestic contractor, which isn't possible with global ones.

near.msg: Those are disadvantages of outsourcing, not advantages.

prompts.q: Give a disadvantage of outsourcing HR functions
prompts.hint: Control, confidentiality, culture... and global contractors bring extra legal headaches.
prompts.learn: Outsourcing hands HR activities to external contractors, so the business risks losing control, expertise and confidentiality. Loss of control can be reduced by negotiating service level agreements (SLAs).

answers.why: The business loses direct control of standards; SLAs (service level agreements) help reduce this.
Sharing confidential staff and company data with outsiders creates privacy risks.
Language or accent issues with global providers can hurt service quality.
Outsourcing a function can mean retrenching the staff who used to do it.
Skills and knowledge leave the business along with the function.
Coordinating activities with an overseas provider is more complex.
Using cheaper overseas labour can raise ethical concerns and damage CSR standing.
A contractor with access to client information may poach clients.
Outsourced staff, not your own, deal with people, so direct contact is lost.

answers.a: No legal remedy under foreign law (global)
answers.why: If a global contractor breaches the contract, remedies under foreign legal systems may be lacking.

near.msg: Those are advantages of outsourcing, not disadvantages.

prompts.q: Name a stakeholder in human resource management
prompts.hint: U GEESE
prompts.learn: HR stakeholders are individuals or groups with an interest in, or affected by, how a business manages its people: Unions, Government organisations, Employees, Employers, Society and Employer associations (U GEESE).

answers.why: Employees provide their labour in exchange for wages and want pay, conditions, security and flexibility.
Employers control and pay employees, negotiate agreements, resolve disputes and manage labour costs.
Unions represent workers to improve wages and conditions, e.g. the TWU or the NSW Teachers Federation.
Government sets the legal framework through legislation, agencies, courts and tribunals (LEGJI).
Society pressures business to act ethically, employ diverse staff and avoid offshoring local jobs.
Groups like Ai Group and ACCI advise employers, bargain for them and lobby government.

near.msg: Not on the HR stakeholder list: it's U GEESE (unions, government, employees, employers, society, employer associations).

prompts.q: Name something employees want from their job
prompts.hint: Money, conditions, security, a say, a future... and a life outside work.
prompts.learn: Employees provide labour in exchange for wages. Beyond pay they want good conditions, security, involvement, career growth and flexibility, which pushes HR to invest in maintaining staff.

answers.why: Pay is the core of the exchange: labour for wages and salaries.
Employees want safe, fair conditions such as reasonable hours and breaks.
Secure employment lets workers plan their finances and lives.
Employees increasingly expect time for family and life outside work.
Many want workplace flexibility such as telecommuting and flexible hours.
Training builds skills and future earning potential.
Employees want to move into higher positions within the business.
Work that feels worthwhile keeps employees engaged.
Being involved in decisions makes staff feel valued and empowered.
Perks like recognition, social activities and development opportunities matter as well as pay.

near.msg: That's what employers want, not employees.

prompts.q: Name a way government influences HRM
prompts.hint: LEGJI
prompts.learn: Government shapes HR through Legislation (e.g. Fair Work Act 2009, WHS Act 2011), Economic policies, Government agencies, the Judicial system and Industrial tribunals (LEGJI).

answers.why: Laws such as the Fair Work Act 2009 and WHS Act 2011 set the rules for employment.
Agencies like the Fair Work Ombudsman and Safe Work NSW implement and enforce the law.
Government economic policy affects growth, demand for labour, inflation and wage growth.
Tribunals like the FWC resolve disputes over issues such as discrimination and unfair dismissal.
The Federal Court hears cases on industrial action, breaches of IR law and common law contracts.

near.msg: Unions are a separate stakeholder, not part of government.

prompts.q: Name a role of the Fair Work Commission
prompts.hint: It's the tribunal: wages, awards, agreements and disputes. Enforcing is someone else's job.
prompts.learn: The Fair Work Commission (FWC) is the independent national workplace relations tribunal set up under the Fair Work Act 2009. It provides a safety net of minimum conditions, approves agreements and decides disputes, but it cannot enforce entitlements or give advice on them.

answers.why: Each year its Annual Wage Review sets a new national minimum wage order.
Agreements must pass the BOOT: employees must be better off overall than under the award.
The FWC makes and varies the modern awards that set minimum industry conditions.
Employees who are dismissed in a harsh, unjust or unreasonable way can apply to the FWC.
It conciliates and, if needed, arbitrates disputes, and hears major cases.

answers.a: Deals with bullying and sexual harassment
answers.why: Workers can apply to the FWC for orders to stop bullying or sexual harassment.
It makes sure employers and employees bargain in good faith for agreements.
It handles claims of discrimination and adverse action against workers.

answers.a: Flexible work and casual conversion disputes
answers.why: It helps with disputes on flexible work, casual to permanent status, parental leave and the right to disconnect.

near.msg: Enforcing pay and entitlements is the Fair Work Ombudsman's job; the FWC can't enforce minimum pay.
The FWC can't advise on award entitlements; the Fair Work Ombudsman educates and advises.

prompts.q: Name a type of employment contract or agreement
prompts.hint: From the industry safety net down to a one-on-one deal.
prompts.learn: An employment contract is a legally binding agreement between employer and employee setting out rights and obligations, and it must meet the National Employment Standards and minimum wage. Pay and conditions may come from awards, enterprise agreements or individual contracts.

answers.why: A safety net of minimum pay, hours, penalty rates, leave loading and allowances for a whole industry.
Negotiated at workplace level, approved by the FWC and must pass the better off overall test.
Negotiated one-on-one, usually for managers; not registered with the FWC, so disputes go to court.
Employment for a set period, ending when the contract expires.
Contractors control their own work and arrange their own tax, super and insurance; no leave.
Ongoing employment with no set end date.
Lets one employee vary award or agreement terms, as long as they are better off overall.
An agreement between two or more employers and groups of their employees.
Made between a union and a new employer that has no employees yet.

near.msg: That's an employment status, not the instrument that sets pay and conditions.

prompts.q: Name a common law obligation of an employer or employee
prompts.hint: Four each. Employer: work, pay, legislation, care. Employee: obey, skill, good faith, notice.
prompts.learn: Common law is law made by courts and judges, as opposed to statute law made by parliament. Every employment contract carries common law obligations for both the employer and the employee.

answers.why: Employer: provide reasonable care and a safe system of work without risks to health.
Employee: refusing lawful, reasonable orders risks dismissal (orders can't expose them to danger).
Employer: pay the income in the award or agreement and reimburse work expenses.
Employee: do the work with care and skill, not negligently.
Employee: give the notice set out in the award, agreement or contract.
Employee: e.g. don't take confidential information to a new employer.
Employer: can't simply stand staff down when it's quiet; must keep paying correct wages.
Employer: meet IR laws such as anti-discrimination, super, workers comp, the NES and awards.

near.msg: Leave is an employee right under the NES and awards, not a common law obligation.

prompts.q: Name a leave entitlement in the National Employment Standards
prompts.hint: The NES are 12 minimum standards in the Fair Work Act. Many of them are leave.
prompts.learn: The Fair Work Act 2009 sets 12 National Employment Standards (NES) that every employee must receive; contracts, awards and agreements cannot go below them. Many of the 12 are leave entitlements.

answers.why: 4 weeks paid leave a year, plus an extra week for some shift workers.
10 days paid personal/carer's leave a year (includes sick leave), plus 2 days unpaid carer's leave.
Up to 12 months unpaid, with the right to request another 12 months.
Extra leave after long service; the rules vary between older awards and modern awards.
A paid day off on each public holiday unless the employer reasonably asks the employee to work.
2 days per occasion when a family or household member dies or is seriously ill (unpaid for casuals).
Unpaid leave for voluntary emergency work, and up to 10 days paid for jury duty.
10 days paid family and domestic violence leave in a 12-month period.

near.msg: That IS one of the 12 NES, just not a leave entitlement. Nice recall.

prompts.q: Name an employer duty under WHS law
prompts.hint: Work Health and Safety Act 2011 (NSW): information, equipment, standards, safe machinery...
prompts.learn: Work health and safety (WHS) means keeping everyone at work safe from hazards and risks. Under the WHS Act 2011 (NSW), employers must keep both the physical environment and employees' emotional wellbeing safe, or face heavy fines and even jail.

answers.why: Employers must supply protective equipment where the work requires it.
Businesses must provide information, instruction, training and supervision.

answers.a: Ensure machinery is safe to use
answers.why: All equipment and machinery must be safe to operate.
Compulsory insurance covers injured workers' medical costs and lost wages.
E.g. safety signs, noise limits and emergency procedures.
Regular audits review the workplace and find hazards before they cause harm.
A safe workplace includes employees' emotional wellbeing, so bullying must be prevented.
A WHS committee brings workers and managers together to consult on safety issues.
Safe Work NSW must be notified of any death or serious injury.

near.msg: That's Fair Work Act territory, not WHS.

prompts.q: Name a way employers meet anti-discrimination and EEO law
prompts.hint: Audit, train, document, report... and treat men and women equally on pay.
prompts.learn: Discrimination is a policy or practice that disadvantages someone because of a characteristic irrelevant to the job, such as age, gender, race, religion, disability, pregnancy or sexual orientation. Equal employment opportunity (EEO) means equitable policies in recruitment, selection, development and promotion.

answers.why: Training managers and staff helps them prevent and deal with discrimination.

answers.a: Equal pay for work of equal value
k: equal pay for men and women
answers.why: Men and women doing work of similar value must get equal pay and conditions.
Recruitment, selection and promotion decisions must be based on merit, free from bias.

answers.a: Code of conduct and written policies
answers.why: Documenting and communicating policies makes clear that discrimination isn't tolerated.
Employers must have grievance procedures so complaints can be raised and resolved.
All policies and practices should be audited to check they are free from discrimination.
Affirmative action removes discrimination and overcomes a lack of equal opportunity for women.
Employers with 100+ staff must report to the Workplace Gender Equality Agency.

near.msg: That's a ground of unlawful discrimination; the prompt wants something an employer does to comply.

prompts.q: Name an effect of economic conditions on HR
prompts.hint: Boom vs bust, high vs low unemployment: who holds the bargaining power?
prompts.learn: Economic influences are macroeconomic conditions (growth, unemployment, inflation, interest rates) that shape the labour market. In a boom or low unemployment workers are scarce and wages rise; in a downturn or high unemployment employers hold the power and may downsize.

answers.why: In an expansion employers compete for workers, pushing wages up.
In a contraction firms cut staff or hours to save costs, and must manage redundancies sensitively.
Booms and low unemployment leave businesses struggling to find enough workers.
High unemployment means more applicants, so HR can be more selective.
With more people competing for fewer jobs, wage growth slows.
Low unemployment gives employees the power; high unemployment gives it to employers.
When jobs are plentiful, employees have more options and leave more easily.

answers.a: Spend more to attract and retain staff
answers.why: In tight markets HR must invest in its employee value proposition, benefits and culture.
In high unemployment staff stay put, but some may be disengaged.

near.msg: That's a technological influence, not an economic one.

prompts.q: Name a technology that is changing HRM
prompts.hint: HEAD
prompts.learn: Technological influences reshape the nature of work, the skills needed and how HR functions are performed. HEAD: HR information systems, E-learning, Automation and AI, Digital communication tools.

answers.why: AI automates routine and increasingly complex tasks, displacing some jobs and creating new ones.
Automation replaces repetitive, predictable tasks and raises demand for higher-skilled roles.
HRIS digitise payroll, leave, appraisal tracking and recruitment, and give real-time workforce data.
Train dispersed workforces at scale, at lower cost and more flexibly than classrooms.
Digital tools changed where, when and how people work, enabling remote and hybrid work.
Video calls let remote and hybrid teams meet without being in the same place.
Cloud tools let staff work on shared files from anywhere.
Messaging apps give fast, informal communication across locations.
Virtual simulations are a digital training tool for practising skills safely.

near.msg: Remote and hybrid work are effects of technology (a changing work pattern), not technologies themselves.

prompts.q: Give an example of a changing work pattern
prompts.hint: Think post-COVID offices, the gig economy and an older, more female workforce.
prompts.learn: Changing work patterns are the evolving ways work is structured, scheduled and performed, driven by technology, employee expectations, globalisation and COVID-19. HR must respond with flexible, forward-thinking people strategies.

answers.why: COVID-19 and digital tools made remote and hybrid work a permanent feature.
More flexibility in the hours and days people work.
Short-term, app-based jobs are a growing non-traditional form of employment.
More people work casually rather than in permanent roles.
Contract and freelance work are growing non-traditional employment forms.
Two or more people share one job, often as part-time arrangements.
Automation and AI are changing the nature of work itself.
The share of women in the workforce keeps rising.
People work longer and ease into retirement, so HR manages an ageing workforce.

near.msg: Standard full-time hours are the traditional pattern, not a change.

prompts.q: Name a way HRM affects employees' living standards
prompts.hint: Four areas: pay, security, safety and wellbeing, careers. Bad practice counts too.
prompts.learn: Living standards are the level of wealth, comfort, goods and necessities available to people. HR decisions on pay, job security, safety and development directly raise or lower employees' living standards.

answers.why: Fair, competitive pay lets employees meet basic needs, support families and take part in the economy.
Secure, permanent work lets people commit to mortgages and investments.
Good WHS protects staff from injury, illness and the financial hardship that follows.
Development lifts earning potential and lets workers move into higher-paid roles.
Poor HR practice like wage theft or underpayment directly lowers living standards.
Over-reliance on casual or gig workers creates income insecurity and financial vulnerability.

near.msg: That's a changing work pattern, the other half of the social influence.

prompts.q: Name a way a business shows ethics and CSR in HRM
prompts.hint: Fair pay, wellbeing, work-life balance, DEI, learning, transparency.
prompts.learn: Ethics and CSR in HRM means applying moral principles to how people are managed, going beyond legal compliance. It lifts motivation, retention and brand image, though it can raise costs in the short term.

answers.why: Offering remote work and flexible hours supports employee wellbeing.
Comprehensive health and wellness programs, including mental health support.

answers.a: Pay a living wage above the minimum
answers.why: Fair employment practice: equitable wages above the legal minimum.
Learning programs and tuition assistance help staff grow.
Parental leave beyond the legal minimum supports work-life balance.
Set measurable DEI targets, build inclusive hiring pipelines and reduce unconscious bias.
Regular pay equity audits close gender and racial wage gaps.
Don't expect staff to answer work contact outside working hours.
Report publicly on turnover, absenteeism, diversity and pay ratios, and allow third-party audits.
Retrain and support employees whose jobs are replaced by automation.

near.msg: Compliance is the legal minimum; ethics and CSR mean going beyond what the law requires.

prompts.q: Name a step in acquiring new staff
prompts.hint: IRS: Identify, Recruit, Select... plus the tools along the way.
prompts.learn: Acquisition is the process of attracting and recruiting the right staff for roles in the business, in three stages: identifying staffing needs, recruitment and selection (IRS). A skills audit and job analysis help define the job before it is advertised.

answers.why: Locating and attracting the right quantity and quality of applicants for vacancies.
Gathering information on each applicant and choosing the most appropriate one.
Analyse internal and external environments to work out how many staff, with what skills.
Job designs and descriptions are developed to guide recruitment.
A systematic study of each employee's duties, tasks and work environment.
Reviews the skills current staff have to reveal gaps that new hires must fill.
New employees usually serve a three-month probation after selection.

near.msg: Induction and training belong to the development process (ITOMP), after acquisition.

prompts.q: Name a selection method used to choose an applicant
prompts.hint: From the paperwork to the final checks.
prompts.learn: Selection involves gathering information about each applicant and determining the most appropriate one. It must be fair and free from discrimination, and the best hire's motivation, goals and values align with the business.

answers.why: A formal discussion to test the applicant's fit, skills and attitude.
The first screen of each applicant's experience and qualifications.
Checks with past employers and background checks confirm the applicant's claims.
Narrowing the field to the best applicants before interviews.
Tests measure skills, aptitude or personality objectively.
Group tasks show how applicants communicate and work in a team.
A three-month probation lets the business confirm the new hire is right for the job.

near.msg: That's recruitment (attracting applicants); selection is choosing between them.

prompts.q: Name a stage in the development of staff
prompts.hint: ITOMP
prompts.learn: Development improves staff skills, abilities and knowledge through Induction, Training, Organisational development, Mentoring and coaching, and Performance appraisal (ITOMP). It lifts productivity, flexibility, motivation and retention.

answers.why: A long-term improvement in skills, knowledge and attributes, on or off the job.
Smooth transition of new staff into the business, making them productive sooner.
Systematic evaluation of strengths, weaknesses and development needs.
Informal: an experienced employee passes knowledge and advice to a less experienced one.
More formal: focused on improving a specific employee's skills and performance.
Develops skills by changing an employee's role, e.g. job rotation or enrichment.

near.msg: Those are acquisition steps (IRS), which come before development.

prompts.q: Name an organisational development or job design method
prompts.hint: Most of them start with 'job'... then think teams.
prompts.learn: Organisational development builds skills by changing an employee's role or responsibilities, while job design shapes a job's content to inform, motivate and retain staff.

answers.why: Moving staff through a variety of jobs to broaden their skill sets.
Increasing the range and breadth of tasks in a job.
Increasing the responsibility and challenge of a role.
Two or more people share the same job, e.g. as part-time arrangements.
Team members make and manage the team's decisions themselves.
Groups given a high level of control over how they organise their work.
Structuring jobs flexibly so staff and tasks can shift as needs change.
Team-based matrix structures that bring together staff from different functions.

near.msg: Those are other development stages; organisational development changes the job itself.

prompts.q: Name a performance appraisal method
prompts.hint: Scales, ratings, rankings, essays, incidents... and a full circle.
prompts.learn: Performance appraisal is the systematic analysis and evaluation of an employee's performance for strengths, weaknesses and development opportunities. Results guide training, promotion and pay decisions, and the records help defend against unfair dismissal claims.

answers.why: A formal discussion between supervisor and employee about performance.
Anonymous feedback from managers, co-workers and subordinates.
The worker rates themselves; in 360-degree feedback this is compared with others' ratings.
Rates traits like reliability, cooperation and quality of work on a scale.
Employees are ranked from best to worst.
A supervisor observes and records evidence of behaviour and performance over time.
The supervisor writes a report on the employee's strengths and weaknesses.
Records how an employee responds in specific situations; often used for supervisors.

near.msg: KPIs are the criteria performance is measured against, not the appraisal method itself.

prompts.q: Name an element of maintaining staff
prompts.hint: FLECR
prompts.learn: Maintenance is the set of processes used to retain staff and manage their wellbeing: Flexible working arrangements, Legal compliance and CSR, Employee participation, Communication and workplace culture, and Rewards (FLECR).

answers.why: Rewards encourage staff to lift productivity and stay with the business.
Flexibility in when, how much and where staff work improves retention.
Regular communication and a supportive culture where staff feel valued.
Involving staff in decisions through meetings, surveys and share plans builds commitment.
Obeying the law is the minimum; CSR means treating staff fairly beyond it.

near.msg: Training and induction are development; recruitment is acquisition. Maintenance is about keeping staff.

prompts.q: Give an advantage of flexible working arrangements
prompts.hint: Motivation, attendance, retention, talent... and rent.
prompts.learn: Flexible working arrangements give employees flexibility in when, how much and where they work, e.g. part-time, job share, compressed weeks, working from home, hybrid work or purchased leave. The Fair Work Act gives some employees the right to request them.

answers.why: Satisfied employees perform better.
Staff can fit work around family and personal commitments.
Reduces costly turnover and re-recruitment.
Employees can manage personal commitments without taking days off.
Attracts people who need flexibility, such as carers.
Remote work reduces the need for office space and facilities.
Shows the business values employee wellbeing.

near.msg: That's a disadvantage of flexible work (supervision, communication, tech costs or equity).

prompts.q: Name a type of voluntary separation
prompts.hint: RRRV
prompts.learn: Separation is the process of ending employment. Voluntary separation is when the employee chooses to leave of their own free will: Resignation, Retirement, Relocation or Voluntary redundancy (RRRV).

answers.why: The employee chooses to leave, often for another job or personal reasons.
Leaving the labour force permanently at the end of a career.
Moving to a new location makes it impossible to keep the job.
Nominating yourself for redundancy during a restructure; appeals to workers near retirement.

near.msg: That's involuntary separation (CIDR): the employee doesn't choose to leave.

prompts.q: Name a type of involuntary separation
prompts.hint: CIDR, and the D splits into SUD.
prompts.learn: Involuntary separation is when an employee is made to leave against their will: Contract expiry, Involuntary redundancy, Dismissal and Retrenchment (CIDR). Dismissal can be Summary, Unfair or on notice (SUD). Redundancy targets positions; retrenchment targets people.

answers.why: Employment is ended for poor performance or a serious breach of contract.
The position is no longer needed, e.g. site closure, new technology or restructuring.
Not enough work for the person, usually in a downturn; the business must show evidence.
Employment ends when a fixed-term contract finishes.
Instant dismissal for a serious breach such as theft or serious misconduct.
Harsh, unjust or unreasonable dismissal; the FWC can order reinstatement or compensation.
For consistently poor performance, after written warnings, support and a chance to respond.

near.msg: That's voluntary separation (RRRV): the employee chooses to leave.

prompts.q: Give an advantage of a leadership style
prompts.hint: LAD: Laissez-faire, Autocratic, Democratic. Each has its own strengths.
prompts.learn: Leadership style is the traits and behaviours a leader uses to lead, motivate and communicate with staff, and it can affect profitability by around 30%. The best style depends on the situation and the skill of the staff.

answers.why: Management decides with little input, so it suits urgent decisions.
Staff are asked for suggestions and may offer valuable insights.
Involvement lifts satisfaction and cuts absenteeism and turnover.
Clear top-down control gives organised, consistent outcomes.
Democratic style focuses on teamwork, collaboration and engagement.
Experienced, skilled self-starters can use their own expertise.
Trusting skilled staff can create a positive work environment.
Effective leadership creates engagement, where employee and business goals align.

near.msg: That's a disadvantage (democratic is slower; autocratic is less open to ideas).
That's the style itself; name one of its advantages, e.g. fast decisions (autocratic).

prompts.q: Give a disadvantage of a leadership style
prompts.hint: LAD: too controlling, too slow, or too hands-off.
prompts.learn: No style suits every situation: autocratic suits unskilled staff and urgent decisions, democratic suits engaged teams, and laissez-faire suits experienced self-starters. Ineffective leadership lowers motivation, morale, productivity and retention.

answers.why: Consulting staff takes time before management makes the final call.
Low empowerment and involvement leave staff dissatisfied.
Dissatisfied, disempowered staff stay away more and leave sooner.
Management decides alone, so other solutions get ignored.
Input from unskilled or inexperienced staff can lead to poorer decisions.
Without direction, teams can split, hurting motivation and morale.
Command responsibility may not be properly defined when managers step back.

near.msg: That's an advantage, not a disadvantage.
That's the style itself; name one of its drawbacks, e.g. slower decisions (democratic).

prompts.q: Name a factor to consider when designing a job
prompts.hint: Variety, responsibility, autonomy... and general vs specific tasks.
prompts.learn: Job design is designing the content of a job and how it fits with other jobs, to inform, motivate and retain staff. General tasks give variety and flexibility; specific tasks give specialisation and efficiency but can be boring.

answers.why: Variety keeps work engaging and builds a more flexible workforce.
How much the employee is accountable for shapes motivation and challenge.
The physical and social setting the job is done in.
How much freedom the employee has to decide how to do the work.
Involvement in decisions increases commitment.
Poorly designed jobs cause boredom, higher turnover and trouble attracting talent.
General tasks build flexible skills; specific tasks build specialisation (scientific management).

near.msg: Pay is set through rewards and awards; job design is about the content and structure of the work.

prompts.q: Give an advantage of internal recruitment
prompts.hint: Known person, known culture, no ad bill.
prompts.learn: Internal recruitment fills vacancies from within the business by transfer, promotion or recommendation. It is quicker, cheaper and less risky, but brings in no new skills or ideas.

answers.why: No advertising or recruitment agency fees.
The candidate is already in the building, so the role is filled quickly.
Promotion opportunities motivate and develop existing staff.
Already familiar with the culture, so they adjust quickly.
The business already knows the employee's strengths and weaknesses.
Staff see a future in the business and become more committed.
Grooming insiders for senior roles keeps leadership continuity.

near.msg: That's an advantage of EXTERNAL recruitment; internal recruitment brings no new skills or ideas.

prompts.q: Give a disadvantage of internal recruitment
prompts.hint: Same people, same ideas... and someone has to fill the gap.
prompts.learn: Internal recruitment promotes or transfers existing staff. Its main weakness is that it adds no new skills, ideas or experiences, and it can create rivalry and a fresh vacancy.

answers.why: Little value is added: no new skills, ideas or experiences come in.
Staff who miss out on the promotion may lose motivation.
Competing for positions lowers teamwork and collaboration.
There may be nobody inside the business who can fill the role.
Recruiting again for the job the candidate leaves can be disruptive and expensive.

answers.a: Keeps old politics and power structures
answers.why: Promoting insiders leaves existing internal politics untouched (external hires shake them up).

near.msg: That's a disadvantage of EXTERNAL recruitment; internal is quicker, cheaper and less risky.

prompts.q: Give an advantage of external recruitment
prompts.hint: Bigger pool, fresh blood.
prompts.learn: External recruitment fills vacancies from outside the business through agencies, online ads, universities and the media. It widens the talent pool and brings new skills and ideas, at greater cost and risk.

answers.why: Outsiders bring skills, ideas and experiences the business doesn't have.
More applicants means a better chance of finding the right person.
Hiring from outside can make the workforce more diverse.

answers.a: Hire someone experienced in the role
answers.why: You may get someone who has done the role elsewhere instead of training an insider.
Unlike promoting from within, no second position is left empty.
An outsider can change internal politics and power structures.

near.msg: That's an advantage of INTERNAL recruitment.

prompts.q: Give a disadvantage of external recruitment
prompts.hint: Unknown person, unknown fit, bigger bill.
prompts.learn: External recruitment brings in people from outside the business. It costs more, takes longer and is riskier because the business doesn't know the person, and new hires need time to adjust.

answers.why: Advertising and recruitment agency fees add up.
Advertising, screening and interviewing outsiders takes time.

answers.a: More risk with an unknown person
answers.why: The business doesn't know the person's real strengths and weaknesses.
New employees may not perform or fit into the business culture.
Productivity is lost while the newcomer is inducted and learns the business.
Existing employees may resent an outsider being brought in over them.

near.msg: That's a disadvantage of INTERNAL recruitment.

prompts.q: Give a benefit of training and developing staff
prompts.hint: Training builds current skills; development builds future ones.
prompts.learn: Training improves employees' current skills for productivity and efficiency, while development builds skills for the future needs of the business and greater responsibility. Both cost time and money, but under-investing leads to poor quality, accidents, low morale and separation.

answers.why: Better-skilled staff work faster and more efficiently.
Training lifts motivation and commitment, at least in the short term.
Staff who feel valued stay, so talent is easier to retain.
Multi-skilled staff can cover more roles and adapt to change.
More satisfied, capable staff give better service, lifting customer satisfaction.
Under-trained staff produce poor quality; training fixes weaknesses.
Motivated, committed staff take fewer days off.
Development readies staff for greater responsibility and future positions.
Insufficient training leads to accidents; well-trained staff work safely.
Developing staff is key to a long-term, sustainable competitive advantage.

near.msg: That's the downside: training and development cost time and money (but under-investing costs more).

prompts.q: Give a purpose of performance management
prompts.hint: Developmental (employee focus) or administrative (organisation focus).
prompts.learn: Performance management is the systematic evaluation and management of employee performance against criteria. Developmental performance management builds the individual; administrative performance management uses aggregate data for organisational decisions such as pay, promotion and strategy.

answers.why: Feedback and recognition make employees feel valued, lowering turnover.
Shows where staff need training and development.
Administrative: results determine eligibility for bonuses and pay rises.
Administrative: identifies who is ready for promotion.
Developmental: uses data to develop each employee's skills and knowledge.
Developmental: prepares staff to take on more responsibility later.
Administrative: aggregate data shows how the business is tracking and where to improve.
Regular appraisal builds a culture of continuous improvement.

answers.a: Records to defend unfair dismissal claims
answers.why: Documented reviews support the separation process and can head off unfair dismissal claims.

near.msg: Performance management assesses current staff; recruitment and selection bring new staff in.

prompts.q: Name a reward an employer can offer staff
prompts.hint: Monetary (financial value) or non-monetary; individual or group.
prompts.learn: Rewards are extra benefits, monetary or non-monetary, given in recognition of service, effort or achievement. Monetary rewards have a financial value; non-monetary rewards cost little; group rewards build team culture; performance pay links income to KPIs.

answers.why: Monetary, individual or group: paid for meeting or exceeding KPIs.
Monetary: a higher salary rewards and helps retain talented staff.
Non-monetary: recognition costs the business little or nothing.
Monetary performance pay: income rises with the sales the employee makes.
Non-monetary: flexibility is highly valued but costs little.
Non-monetary: development, extra responsibility and new challenges.
Monetary: staff share in the business's profits.
Monetary benefits paid in a form other than wages, such as a car or gym membership.
Monetary: staff become part-owners, aligning them with the business.
Group reward: if team-based profitability rises, team members share the gain.

near.msg: Those are legal entitlements (NES or award), not rewards for effort.

prompts.q: Give an advantage of using overseas staff or contractors
prompts.hint: Global strategies tackle costs, skills and supply.
prompts.learn: Global HR strategies deal with Australia's high labour costs, skill shortages and limited domestic labour supply, e.g. offshoring to China or India or hiring on temporary skilled visas. The trade-offs are communication problems, training needs and possible brand damage.

answers.why: Countries like China have lower minimum wages than Australia.
Specialist overseas labour can improve the quality of outsourced work.
Countries such as India have a large supply of workers.
Temporary work visas bring in skilled workers for shortage areas like IT and health.
A culturally diverse workforce is also a CSR positive.
Global HR contractors may offer more advanced technology and faster service.
India offers a highly educated, English-speaking workforce for IT, legal, accounting and call centres.
Besides lower wages, some countries have minimal on-costs such as payroll tax and super.

near.msg: That's a disadvantage of using overseas staff.

prompts.q: Name a cause of workplace disputes
prompts.hint: Pay, security, safety, change... and unpopular management decisions.
prompts.learn: A workplace dispute is a disagreement between an employer and employees that remains unresolved. Disputes cost productivity, morale, staff and reputation, and resolving them is slow and expensive, so high disputation signals poor HRM.

answers.why: A breakdown in pay negotiations is a major cause of disputes.
Poor conditions or WHS issues spark disputes.
Downsizing and restructuring threaten jobs and anger staff.
Fear of losing jobs is a common trigger for disputes.
Sending work to contractors or offshore threatens existing jobs.
Common grievances that can escalate into disputes.
Unpopular management policies and decisions cause disagreement.
Missed promotions and unfavourable promotion decisions lead to grievances.
Unfavourable decisions about hours and work-life balance cause disputes.
A personality clash with a co-worker is a classic grievance example.

near.msg: Industrial action is a result of a dispute, not a cause.

prompts.q: Name a way to resolve a workplace dispute
prompts.hint: From cheap and informal to a binding order: N, M, C, A... plus grievance procedures and the courts.
prompts.learn: Disputes are escalated step by step: negotiation (no third party), mediation (neutral third party), then FWC conciliation (suggests solutions) and arbitration (legally binding order). Grievance procedures resolve issues internally first; courts handle breaches of IR law and common law contracts.

answers.why: Cheap, fast and flexible with no third party, but not guaranteed and not binding.
A neutral third party facilitates; cheaper than tribunals but non-binding.
Formal internal steps, usually set out in the award or agreement, to resolve issues quickly.
A tribunal makes a legally binding, enforceable decision; costly and neither party controls the outcome.
An FWC conciliator suggests solutions but doesn't impose a decision.
Tribunals like the FWC step in when negotiation and mediation fail.
For breaches of IR law, serious industrial action or common law contract disputes.

near.msg: Industrial action is a symptom of a dispute, not a way to resolve it.

prompts.q: Name a form of industrial action
prompts.hint: Some are overt (obvious), some covert (hidden).
prompts.learn: Industrial action is collective action taken in a workplace dispute, either overt (obvious) or covert (hidden). It causes lost productivity, disrupted supply and negative publicity.

answers.why: Overt: employees stop work altogether.
Overt: striking workers block deliveries, staff and employers from the workplace.
Overt: the employer refuses to let employees into the workplace.
Overt: employees deliberately work at a slower rate.
Overt: employees refuse to do a certain part of their work.
Overt: employees refuse to do anything beyond their basic duties.
Covert: hidden damage to the business's operations.
Covert: staff quietly stay away from work.

near.msg: That's a way to resolve a dispute, not industrial action.

prompts.q: Name an indicator of HR effectiveness
prompts.hint: CLAW ABC
prompts.learn: HR effectiveness is judged by CLAW ABC: Corporate culture, Levels of disputation, Absenteeism, Worker satisfaction, Accidents, Benchmarking key variables and Changes in staff turnover.

answers.why: The share of staff leaving over a period; Australia averages 12-15% a year.
High absenteeism signals HRM problems and costs productivity.
Measured through satisfaction surveys and feedback over time.
More accidents mean higher workers comp premiums, lost productivity and lower morale.
The shared values, ideas and expectations of staff.
High levels of disputes show a poor employer-employee relationship.
Comparing HR indicators internally or with other businesses to find areas to improve.

near.msg: Those are financial or marketing measures; HR effectiveness is measured by CLAW ABC.

prompts.q: Name a possible cause of absenteeism
prompts.hint: Stress, balance, attitude, home life, satisfaction, motivation, culture.
prompts.learn: Absenteeism is when an employee is absent from work, with or without a genuine reason; sick leave costs Australian businesses about $7 billion a year. High absenteeism signals problems with HRM and costs productivity.

answers.why: A genuine reason, though absences may or may not be genuine.
Stressed staff are more likely to take days off.
Unmotivated employees find reasons not to come in.
Dissatisfied workers disengage and stay away.
Staff who can't balance work and life take time off to cope.
Personal and family pressures pull people away from work.
A poor culture and low morale make people avoid work.
High absenteeism and turnover can indicate boredom in the job.
Poor employee-management relationships show up as absenteeism.
Some staff see sick leave as owed to them and take it whether sick or not.

near.msg: Planned leave is an entitlement, not absenteeism.

prompts.q: Name a cost or effect of high staff turnover
prompts.hint: Follow a leaver out the door and a new hire in.
prompts.learn: Staff turnover is the number or percentage of employees who leave over a period; it is higher in retail and hospitality. High turnover is expensive and signals dissatisfaction and a problem with HRM, though some turnover brings in fresh ideas.

answers.why: Every leaver has to be replaced through recruitment.
New staff need training and development to reach full performance.
Gaps and inexperienced replacements reduce output.
Constant departures damage corporate culture and morale.
Each new hire must be inducted, using staff time and money.
Extra costs and lost productivity eat into profit.
Leavers take knowledge, skills and competencies with them.
Separations can involve redundancy and termination payments.
High turnover shows staff are dissatisfied and there is a problem with HRM.
Customers and suppliers lose their familiar contacts, straining relationships.

near.msg: That's the upside: some turnover brings in new ideas, skills and experience.

prompts.q: Name a type of benchmarking
prompts.hint: PIBB
prompts.learn: Benchmarking compares HR indicators such as labour costs, disputes, turnover, absenteeism, accidents and worker satisfaction between sections of the business or against other businesses, so areas for improvement can be found and corrective action taken.

answers.why: Comparing against the leading businesses in the industry and copying their processes.
Comparing performance levels of a process or activity with other businesses.
Comparing HR indicators against other businesses.
Networking, visiting other businesses, researching best practice online and attending conferences.
Comparing indicators between sections of the same business.
Comparing performance with the objectives in the business's strategic plan.

near.msg: That's a variable you benchmark, not a type of benchmarking.
